transcript:
Meeting Header: 2026-03-12 16:00 UTC | Duration ~45 mins
Attendees: Lydia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Jorge Alvarez (Redwood CSM); Rachel Moore (NexaHealth CTO), Ian Park (ML Eng), Sofia Reyes (Infra), Daniel Kim (SRE)

Summary (auto): Quick recap of benchmark numbers vs baseline provider, dig into p99 tail, discuss tuning recommendations, next steps.

[00:00] Lydia Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we did a quick agenda — benchmark highlights, p99 tail deep-dive, tuning recommendations, next steps. Rachel you good to kick off?
[00:17] Rachel Moore: yeah thanks Lydia, quick context — we ran the Redwood-built harness against our current baseline provider, focus was 512 and 1k token scenarios, mixed user profiles, and peak qps. seeing some interesting numbers, so want to walk through.
[00:38] Marcus Patel: perfect, i'll share screen with the spreadsheet, i'm bringing up the p50/p95/p99 plots — if anyone can't see ping in chat.
[00:52] Ian Park: we can see the spreadsheet, small delay on the plots loading.
[01:05] Marcus Patel: ok so for the 1k token synthetic run, median latency on Redwood hosted was ~420ms vs baseline 610ms. throughput at target qps of 120 rps sustained for 15 minutes was better on Redwood, about 10-12% higher. those are median and avg numbers, the p99 is where we saw the mismatch — Redwood p99 at ~1.8s vs baseline ~2.6s.
[01:38] Daniel Kim: right that's a big gap, but the p99 spike — what's driving that? network or the model runtime?
[01:45] Marcus Patel: good question. initial breakdown shows two contributors: network jitter for some nodes (we saw spikes correlated with cross-az hop) and occasional kernel fallback when sequence length exceeded the precompiled path, which triggers a slower code path.
[02:03] Lydia Chen: just to add, our kv/prefix cache reduced token generation work for repeated prefixes, so steady-state throughput improves. but cache misses and cold starts still hit the slower path.
[02:18] Sofia Reyes: we noticed some outliers on our end — one of our test agents was in eu-central while most traffic was us-east, so that may explain cross-region tail. we'll run a controlled run next week.
[02:32] Rachel Moore: Marcus, can you explain the kernel fallback — is that something we can tune or is it model-level?
[02:39] Marcus Patel: yeah so quickie: our runtime selects kernels based on architecture and sequence length distribution. when sequences go beyond the optimized tile size for the quantized kernel, it falls back to a more generic kernel. we can recompile or pick a different quant profile to reduce fallback rate. also changing batch sizing helps.
[02:58] Ian Park: are there safety or accuracy tradeoffs with re-quantizing? we can't degrade output quality.
[03:06] Marcus Patel: totally understood. we tested int8 and int4 profiles; int8 preserves fidelity mostly, int4 has some small regressions on a handful of prompts. we can run targeted evals on your prompt set first — that's what Redwood Optimize would suggest.
[03:23] Rachel Moore: ok that's helpful. on throughput, can you explain the 10% improvement — is that purely batching and caching?
[03:30] Marcus Patel: largely yes. continuous batching in the runtime and smarter kernel selection, plus prefix caching for repeated contexts. Also our smart routing avoided some saturated nodes that baseline provider had in their pool during the run.
[03:45] Lydia Chen: and to be explicit on cost implications — higher throughput with similar per-GPU utilization means lower $/request in many cases. i'll put together a pricing delta for hosted vs dedicated for the pilot qps.
[03:56] Rachel Moore: great.
[04:02] -- Topic shift: p99 tail deep dive --
[04:05] Marcus Patel: here's the p99 scatter, you can see clusters where network latency and the fallback kernel line up. we also saw a small percentage of requests hitting a GC pause on our side — rare but visible in the logs.
[04:22] Daniel Kim: GC pause? in the runtime? can you point to the trace id?
[04:26] Marcus Patel: i'll paste trace ids in the shared doc, but it's more an internal buffer flush in the host process when memory pressure spikes for a batch. we tuned allocator thresholds in our next run and it reduced occurrences.
[04:40] Sofia Reyes: for the network tests, we'll run from same-eu, same-us, and cross-region to isolate. also want to confirm TLS offload and LB settings, those can add a few hundred ms.
[04:53] Lydia Chen: good call — Sofia if you can run that, we'll align and re-run the benchmark.
[05:00] Rachel Moore: what's your recommendation for immediate p99 mitigation?
[05:04] Marcus Patel: short term: pin nodes to same region, increase small-batch target to reduce kernel fallback, enable aggressive KV cache warmup for the demo windows. medium term: we can recompile kernels for your seq distribution or test int8 profile with shadow evals.
[05:20] Ian Park: shadow evals meaning run int8 in parallel and compare outputs?
[05:24] Marcus Patel: yes run int8 inference side-by-side, score against your eval set; no visible user impact in most cases.
[05:33] Rachel Moore: ok, and the baseline provider — were there any wins they had versus you?
[05:37] Marcus Patel: baseline had slightly better p95 in a couple runs; likely because they had more aggressive pre-warming in their pool. but their p99 and median were both higher overall. baseline also had less transparency into kernel selection which made tuning slower.
[05:54] Lydia Chen: also note baseline's pricing model had hidden egress and storage costs that inflated at our simulated scale — i'll include a clear per-request calc.
[06:07] Rachel Moore: fine. on security/compliance — quick check, is the audit log and KMS flow available in hosted? we need SOC2 artefacts.
[06:16] Lydia Chen: yes hosted provides audit logs, KMS integration for keys, and we have SOC2 report; i'll share the security pack after the call.
[06:26] Rachel Moore: thanks.
[06:30] Marcus Patel: ok back to tuning notes — i recommend these concrete steps: 1) re-run with same-region agents, 2) bump batch sizing for long seqs, 3) run int8 shadow eval on your dev prompts, 4) enable KV cache pre-warm for repeated user contexts.
[06:46] Sofia Reyes: we can try 1 and 2 this week, 3 will require ML sign-off but likely doable.
[06:52] Lydia Chen: perfect. we'll queue up Marcus to upload the detailed p99 plots and raw logs.
[07:00] -- People ask some clarifying questions, slight crosstalk --
[07:05] Ian Park: one more thing, did you compare cost per 1M tokens?
[07:09] Lydia Chen: yes a quick calc — with current batching and KV, Redwood hosted cost per 1M tokens is about 12% lower than baseline at the observed throughput; dedicated reduces cost further but requires commit.
[07:22] Rachel Moore: how much commitment for dedicated? ballpark.
[07:25] Lydia Chen: i'll put numbers in the pricing doc, but typically monthly reserved pools start at ~$Xk for the pilot (we'll specify).
[07:33] Daniel Kim: we also need to test failure behaviour — how does Redwood degrade when a node goes down? fallbacks?
[07:39] Marcus Patel: there are automatic fallbacks: routing to healthy nodes and model variant fallback if capacity low; we can show a demo of a simulated outage next sync.
[07:50] Rachel Moore: great.
[07:54] Lydia Chen: ok shall we recap next steps? Marcus will upload plots & logs; Lydia to share pricing and security pack; Sofia to run network tests; Rachel to confirm success criteria.
[08:06] Rachel Moore: yes, and we'll aim to re-run the benchmark Wed next week once Sofia runs network tests.
[08:12] Lydia Chen: sounds good, thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with links.

End transcript.

References/Artifacts Shared: link:shared-drive/reports/nexa-bench-2026-03-12.xlsx ; link:shared-drive/trace-ids/trace-03-12.log ; security-pack/soc2-summary.pdf
